title: Why do we need commandments?
summary: The Bible distinguishes the moral law (the Ten Commandments - enduring, because it expresses God's character) from the ceremonial law of Moses (which pointed to Christ and was fulfilled in him). Keeping the commandments is not legalism, but obedience born of love and in the power of the Spirit - relationship before rules.

sections.heading: Does a Christian Still Have Commandments?

items.comment: Jesus says plainly that he did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it. "To fulfill" does not mean "to cancel" - it means "to give full meaning."

questions.text: What does Jesus rule out here, and what does he affirm regarding the Law?

items.label: "to fulfill" (plēroō)
items.content: In Matt 5:17 Jesus uses *plēroō* - "to fill, to complete, to bring to fullness." This is not the same as "to abolish" (Greek *katalyō*, which Jesus explicitly denies). The verb points to giving the Law its full meaning, not to doing away with it.

questions.text: How does distinguishing *plēroō* (to complete) from *katalyō* (to abolish) bring order to the debate over the law's permanence?

items.comment: Paul, the apostle of grace, asks: does faith nullify the Law? And he answers: on the contrary - it upholds it. Grace does not abolish the law, but restores it to its proper place.

questions.text: How is it possible that faith "upholds" the law rather than abolishing it?

items.comment: The law is "holy, righteous, and good." The problem was never the law, but our heart - which is why we need not the abolition of the law, but a transformation of the heart.

questions.text: If the law is good, where does the problem of sin really lie?

items.label: "Law" is the Hebrew tora ("instruction")
items.content: The most common Old Testament word for "law" is *tora* - "direction, instruction, guidance," not merely a dry "regulation." In the New Testament it is rendered by the Greek *nomos*. That is why "law" in the Bible can be a broad term for the whole revealed will of God, and not just a list of prohibitions - which explains why Paul says that faith "upholds" the law rather than abolishing it.

questions.text: How does the debate over "the law" change when we understand it as "instruction" rather than just a "statute"?

sections.heading: Two Kinds of Law: Moral and Ceremonial

items.comment: The law written by Moses was placed BESIDE the ark. The Ten Commandments, on the other hand, God wrote with his own finger, and they were placed INSIDE the ark - the Bible distinguishes these two collections even in the way they were stored.

questions.text: What might the difference mean: the law of Moses beside the ark, and the Ten Commandments within it?

items.label: two collections of laws and the ark
items.content: In the Bible the Ten Commandments ("ten words") are placed inside the ark (Exod 25:16; Deut 10:5), while the "book of the Law" written by Moses is placed beside it (Deut 31:26). This difference in where each was stored is sometimes read as pointing to the different status of the moral and the ceremonial law.

items.comment: The Ten Commandments were written "by the finger of God" on stone. This underscores their uniqueness and permanence - they come directly from God.

questions.text: Why do the material (stone) and the author (God himself) underscore the permanence of the Ten Commandments?

items.label: "ten words" (the Ten Commandments)
items.content: "Decalogue" means in Hebrew, literally, "ten words" (cf. Exod 34:28). These ten Words of God were the only part of the Torah proclaimed amid thunder and lightning from the mountain, and then written by the finger of God himself on two tablets of stone (Exod 31:18; Deut 4:13; 10:4). These exceptional circumstances of their origin set the moral law apart from the rest of Israel's regulations.

items.comment: The law of sacrifices was "a shadow of the good things to come," and not the reality itself. A shadow vanishes when the thing that cast it appears - namely Christ.

questions.text: Why does a shadow lose its meaning when the reality it foreshadowed arrives?

items.comment: Paul speaks of regulations "concerning festivals, new moons, and [ceremonial] sabbaths" that were a shadow - the substance is Christ. He is speaking of the ceremonial system of sacrifices and festivals, fulfilled in Jesus.

questions.text: What does it mean that the ceremonial regulations were a "shadow," while the "substance" is Christ?

items.label: "shadow" (skia) versus "substance" (sōma)
items.content: Col 2:17 contrasts *skia* (shadow) with *sōma* (body, reality). The ceremonial regulations are a shadow cast ahead by the coming reality - Christ. When the *sōma* arrives, the shadow loses its function, for it has completed its task of pointing forward.

original.text: σκιὰ … τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ
original.translit: skia … to de sōma tou Christou

items.label: "he erased the record of debt against us" (cheirographon)
items.content: The word Paul renders as the record "against us" that was canceled and "nailed to the cross" (Col 2:14) is the Greek *cheirographon* - "a handwritten certificate of debt, a bond of obligation." It occurs only here in the New Testament. What Jesus figuratively nailed to the cross is our condemnation and the debt incurred through sin, together with the system of ceremonial "decrees" (Greek *dogma*) - and not the eternal moral law.

questions.text: What exactly was "nailed to the cross" according to the context of Col 2 - and what does it NOT refer to?

items.label: "sabbaths" in Col 2:16
items.content: In Col 2:16 the list (festivals, new moons, "sabbaths") refers to the calendar of Israel's ceremonial feasts (cf. Lev 23), including the annual festival days called sabbaths, which were tied to the sacrificial system. The text concerns this ceremonial cycle, whose role Christ fulfilled, and not the weekly commandment of the Ten Commandments - which is the subject of a separate study.

items.comment: Christ abolished "the law of commandments expressed in ordinances," which divided Jews and Gentiles - the ceremonial system. The wall of division falls because its role has been fulfilled.

questions.text: Which law divided people into "insiders" and "outsiders," and why could it disappear?

items.comment: John calls Jesus "the Lamb of God." Thousands of lambs offered in sacrifice pointed toward this one moment - when the true Lamb arrives, the foreshadowing is fulfilled.

questions.text: If all the sacrifices pointed to Jesus, what happens to them once he has come?

items.comment: The gifts, sacrifices, and ceremonial regulations were in force "until the time of reformation." They had their term - they pointed further on, toward Christ.

questions.text: What does it mean that these regulations were in force "until the time of reformation"?

items.comment: The former ordinance is set aside because of its weakness - it brought nothing to perfection. In its place comes a better hope: direct access to God through Jesus.

questions.text: What could the old system not give, that Jesus does?

items.label: "guardian leading to Christ" (paidagogos)
items.content: In Gal 3:24 the law is called a "guardian" leading to Christ - the Greek *paidagogos*. In antiquity the *paidagogos* was not a teacher (Greek *didaskalos*), but a slave who escorted a boy to school, protected him, and watched over him. Note that what is in view here is the whole ceremonial system, which was meant to lead to Christ - and when he came, that role was completed.

questions.text: How does the role of a "guide leading to Christ" differ from the role of the "goal," who is Christ himself?

sections.heading: What Is Binding on a Christian

items.comment: When asked about the way to life, Jesus points to specific commandments of the Ten Commandments. After the cross, no one cites the regulations about sacrifices as a rule of life - but the moral commandments remain a point of reference.

questions.text: Why, when speaking about life, does Jesus reach precisely for the commandments of the Ten Commandments?

items.label: "commandments" (entolē), not sacrifices
items.content: To the rich young man Jesus lists specifically: do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness - that is, the Ten Commandments. The word used here is the Greek *entolē* ("commandment"), the same one John uses for God's commandments. Note that the young man kept them legalistically, as a code in itself, but lacked the Lawgiver: "Follow me."

items.comment: James, writing after the cross, still treats the Ten Commandments (murder, adultery) as a "law of freedom" by which we will be judged. The moral law is still binding.

questions.text: Why does James call the law that is still binding a "law of freedom" rather than of slavery?

items.label: "the royal law," "the law of freedom"
items.content: James calls the Ten Commandments "the royal law" and "the law of freedom," by which judgment will be carried out (James 2:8-12). Although salvation is by faith in the cross, judgment relates to the law. Note that slavery does not come from the law - it comes from surrendering to sin; while justification comes from mercy, for "mercy triumphs over judgment" (James 2:13).

items.comment: The sign that we truly know God is keeping his commandments. This is not merit, but evidence of an authentic relationship.

questions.text: How does "keeping the commandments as evidence of relationship" differ from "earning merit by the commandments"?

items.comment: At the close of history, God's people are described as those who "keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus." Commandments and faith are not opposites - they go together.

questions.text: How are we to understand the joining of "the commandments of God" and "the faith of Jesus" in one description?

sections.heading: Obedience Born of Love, in the Power of the Spirit - Not Legalism

items.comment: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments." The order is crucial: first love, and out of it flows obedience - not the other way around.

questions.text: What changes when obedience flows from love rather than coming before it?

items.comment: What the law could not do because of our weakness, God does through the Spirit - so that "the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us." Obedience is the work of the Spirit in us, not our solitary effort.

questions.text: By whose power is the law fulfilled in the life of a believer, according to this text?

items.comment: Salvation is by grace, not by works - and yet we are created "for good works." Works are not the root of salvation, but its fruit.

questions.text: Where in this text is there room for works, since salvation is free?

items.comment: What counts is "faith working through love." This is the biblical remedy for legalism: not a dead rule, but faith that expresses itself in love.

questions.text: How do you tell "faith working through love" apart from the empty keeping of rules?

items.comment: God promises a new heart and his own Spirit, who will cause us to "walk according to his commandments." The transformation begins from within - from God, not from gritted teeth.

questions.text: What does God promise to change first - behavior or the heart? Why does that matter?

items.label: "to do" (poieō) versus "to fulfill" (plēroō) the law
items.content: Note that Paul deliberately uses two different verbs. Of the ceremonial regulations he says "to do" (Greek *poieō*) - the emphasis falls on human effort. Of the moral law and the "law of Christ" he says "to fulfill" (Greek *plēroō*, e.g. Gal 5:14) - the emphasis falls on the work of the Spirit. Obedience to the Ten Commandments becomes complete not through gritted teeth, but as the fruit of the Spirit.

questions.text: Why is distinguishing "to do" (my effort) from "to fulfill" (the work of the Spirit) a remedy for legalism?

application.text: The Bible knows no conflict between grace and law. The ceremonial law - sacrifices, festivals, rites - was a shadow that pointed to Christ and was fulfilled in him. The moral law, the Ten Commandments, endures, because it describes the unchanging character of God. But keeping the commandments is never a way to earn love. It is the fruit of relationship: we love, and so we obey - and not by our own strength, but by the power of the Spirit, who gives a new heart. Relationship always comes before rules.
application.challenge: This week do a simple heart-check: choose one commandment and ask whether you keep it out of fear or obligation, or out of love for God. Ask the Holy Spirit to change your motivation from "I have to" into "I want to."
